newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao temporarily spared court appearance.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao temporarily spared court appearance.

text.p: India's Supreme Court ruled that former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao did not have to appear at a lower court hearing on Monday in a criminal conspiracy case.

A two-judge panel said Rao was exempted from having to appear personally in the $100,000 case until it meets on October 7 to decide on a government demand that the venue of the lower court hearing be shifted to a more secure location.
A lower court judge had ordered Rao to appear on Monday to face charges and possible arrest in the 13-year-old case of criminal conspiracy to cheat. Rao says he is innocent.

Late last week the federal government, fearing a security lapse, asked the Supreme Court to move the scheduled hearing from a local court complex to a nearby sports stadium, a cavernous exhibition hall or a modern convention centre.

Supreme Court justices M.M. Puncshi and K.T. Thomas said that "Narasimha Rao, who stands summoned as an accused in the court of Ajit Bharihoke for today, stands exempted from personal appearance and he is permitted to appear through counsel."

Judge Bharihoke had set Monday's hearing for 2 p.m. (0830 GMT) in the Tis Hazari court complex, which was surrounded by hundreds of police and journalists. The session was expected to go ahead without Rao.

The lower court could still indict Rao and order him held in custody pending trial, authorities said. Although Rao was denied legal protection against arrest last week, he could immediately seek bail if charged and detained.
Rao, who quit in disgrace as Congress party leader on September 21 after a court upheld a summons in the case, would be the first former prime minister to appear in court in a criminal case.
A court sentenced Indira Gandhi for contempt of parliament in 1978, but the charges were not criminal in nature.
If arrested and denied bail, Rao would be put in either judicial or police custody pending completion of the trial, court officials said.

Tihar jail, Asia's biggest prison with some 10,000 inmates, was prepared to take in Rao. But there was also the possibility he would be detained in his home or at another residential site, authorities said.
As a diabetic with a history of heart problems, Rao would need special medical supervision.

At issue in the case were allegations by an expatriate Indian businessman that Rao and a Hindu guru conspired to cheat him out of $100,000 in 1983, when Rao was foreign minister. The guru, Chandraswami, and his personal assistant are currently in judicial custody awaiting trial.

Last Thursday, federal police filed charges against Rao in a separate forgery case involving an alleged attempt in 1989 to tarnish the reputation of V.P. Singh, an opposition leader who later became prime minister.
Rao's legal woes forced a change of guard at the top of the Congress party, which suffered its worst ever defeat in the general elections that ended in May.

The political turmoil sent shock waves through India's stock markets, which anticipated trouble for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government. Congress offers Deve Gowda's minority coalition make-or-break support in parliament.
